
### networks / hosts aka end systems 



::: {.r-stack .my-full}

![](/intro/texfig/nodes-links-networks.figure-1.svg){.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=2 fig-alt="Picture showing computers connected via lines with arrowheads on both ends to a cloud."}

![](/intro/texfig/nodes-links-networks.figure-2.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2 fig-alt="Same diagram as previous slide. The cloud is highlighted and labeled as a ‘network’."}

![](/intro/texfig/nodes-links-networks.figure-3.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4 fig-alt="Same diagram as previous slide. The computers are labeled ‘hosts’."}

::: {.myoverbox .highright .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}

_networks_ connect computers.

:::

::: {.myoverbox .highright .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}

the cloud represents any network (whether local or not)

this iconography predates cloud computing

:::

::: {.myoverbox .highright .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3}

computers on the edge of a network are called _hosts_ or _end systems_

(even if also "servers")

:::

### switches / nodes / links 



::: {.r-stack .my-full}
![](/intro/texfig/nodes-links-switches.figure-1.svg){.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=2 fig-alt="Diagram of computers connected by a network. Lines with arrowheads at both ends extend from the computers to a number of boxes (with a design of crossing lines with arrowheads). Later frames repeat the diagram and indicate the boxes are called ‘switches’; every participant (computers and switches) are called ‘nodes’; and the lines connecting them are called ‘links’ (regardless of whether implemented with wires or radio or whatever)."}

![](/intro/texfig/nodes-links-switches.figure-2.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2 fig-alt="Same diagram with switches highlighted."}

![](/intro/texfig/nodes-links-switches.figure-3.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3 fig-alt="Same diagram with all machines (switches and normal computers) highlighted."}

![](/intro/texfig/nodes-links-switches.figure-4.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4 fig-alt="Same diagram with links (all connections between machines, which are point-to-point in the diagram) highlighted."}

:::

::: {.myoverbox .highright .fragment fragment-index=2 .fade-in-then-out}

hosts directly connected <br/>
to _switches_<br/>

implement network more efficient <br/>
than shared medium

:::

::: {.myoverbox .highright .fragment fragment-index=3 .fade-in-then-out}

machines on network <br/>
(hosts, switches, ...) <br/>
called _nodes_

:::

::: {.myoverbox .highright .fragment fragment-index=4 .fade-in-then-out}

nodes connected by <br/>
_links_ 

(implemented by wires <br/>
or radio or ...)

:::

connected networks form<br/>
_internetwork_<br/><br/>
example: the Internet

:::


### routers versus switches {.smaller}

*  _router_ versus _switch_ division not so clear in practice
*  historically "easy"
   *  router uses internetwork protocol like IP to forward data
      *  IP = Internet Protocol
   *  switches does not understand IP (just copies bits for IP)
*  but lots of things called "switches" that implement IP now
   *  example: most datacenter "top-of-rack switches"
*  this class default:
   *  switch = "layer 2" like Ethernet
   *  router = "layer 3" --- IP
   *  if both --- we'll treat as one box containing switch(es) + router
